item.title: The True Origins Behind America’s Most Famous National Park Ghost Stories
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
Writer Lauren Liebhaber lives in Salem, Massachusetts, and loves Halloween more than most. She is a spooky season expert. For this story, she dug into the legends of ghost stories in some of the country’s most popular national parks. From a headless bride in the Old Faithful Inn to phantom hikers in the Grand Canyon, she researched five haunting tales, their origins and the truth behind them. National parks are fertile ground for storytelling. These lands hold deep geological, cultural and sacred histories stretching back thousands of years, and places like this have a way of inspiring and collecting stories. They get passed around and retold, with old details dropped and new ones added until the story itself becomes a sort of Frankenstein’s monster. Fact and folklore blend together until it’s hard to tell where history ends and legend begins. And national parks have no shortage of settings for the unexplained. They’re full of dark caves, old buildings, abandoned settlements, battlefields and vast stretches of wilderness. Spend a night at the bottom of a canyon or in a century-old hotel, and every unexplained footstep, flicker of light or movement in your periphery starts to feel a little more…otherworldly. So it’s probably no surprise that some of the stories we’ve attached to these places involve ghosts. What is surprising is where some of those stories came from. Old Faithful Inn is a gabled monument to lodgepole pine. Opened in 1904, it was built for people who wanted to watch Old Faithful erupt, then retire somewhere a little more comfortable, but still suitably rustic. It has character, and if you ask the right person, it was also home to Yellowstone’s most famous murder. Here’s one version of the story. It’s 1915, and the rebellious teenage daughter of a wealthy New York shipping magnate has refused an arranged marriage. Who could blame her? She’s fallen for an older man who works in their house as a servant. Her father, however, is certain the man is after the family fortune, so, in an attempt to call their bluff, he makes the couple an offer: Take a generous dowry, leave New York and never come back. The newlyweds take the money and head west, eventually arriving at Old Faithful Inn for their honeymoon. In some tellings, they stay in Room 127. At first, things seem fine. Then the husband starts drinking and gambling, burning through the dowry until, about a month in, they’re broke. The bride calls her father for help, but he says no. One night, hotel staff hear the couple fighting. The husband storms out of the room and is never seen again. For a couple of days, the staff keep their distance. Finally, a worried maid enters the room and finds the bride in the bathroom, covered in blood. Her head is gone. They search the inn for days before, according to the legend, someone finally looks up. There, in the Crow’s Nest—the perch high above the lobby where musicians once played for evening dances—is the bride’s missing head. And that’s where people say she still appears. Over the years, guests and employees have described a woman in white drifting down from the Crow’s Nest, sometimes carrying her own severed head. In other versions, she walks the halls at midnight, all the way back to the room where she was murdered on her honeymoon. It’s a gruesome story. And it is also completely made up. Yellowstone’s staff have traced one version of the story to former Old Faithful Inn bell captain George Bornemann. A reporter was apparently pestering Bornemann for the inn’s ghost stories. Bornemann repeatedly told him there weren’t any, but the reporter was relentless. So Bornemann made one up. When the reporter asked what year the murder had happened, Bornemann reportedly told him to pick whatever year he liked. There’s also a second version of the confession. According to the company that operates Yellowstone’s lodges, an assistant manager from the 1980s told a newspaper in 1991 that he’d invented the story because guests always expected a historic hotel to have a ghost. Whether two employees independently had the same idea, or the storyteller’s identity changed as the tale was retold, isn’t entirely clear. The fact that people claim to see the ghastly ghost of this fictitious beheaded bride shows this story is an impressive testament to the power of the human imagination in more ways than one. Mammoth Cave doesn’t need fictional ghosts. Its documented history is unsettling enough. In the fall of 1842, a Kentucky doctor named John Croghan, who had purchased Mammoth Cave a few years earlier, wondered whether its environment might help cure tuberculosis. The cave was cool, the air seemed pristine and the miners who spent long stretches underground appeared to be in good health. At a time when tuberculosis was killing huge numbers of people and medicine had little to offer, Croghan hypothesized that living inside Mammoth Cave might give damaged lungs a chance to heal. So he moved 16 tuberculosis patients underground to test his theory. About a mile and a half into the cave, Croghan created a subterranean settlement with wooden cottages and stone buildings. Patients spent their days entirely underground, living by lamplight and candlelight. One resident wrote that he hardly ever heard daylight mentioned, or even thought of it. They were told the cave might save them. Sadly, it didn’t. Fires used for warmth and cooking filled the still cave with smoke, and the patients became sicker. Alfred, an enslaved man who worked as a cave guide, later recalled the residents looking like a company of skeletons with pupils so dilated by the darkness that their eyes appeared black. Some patients died underground. Within months, Croghan abandoned his experiment. The stone structures are still there and, according to generations of visitors, so is the coughing. People have reported hearing coughs near the old tuberculosis settlement when nobody is there. It’s an easy legend to understand. People really did cough, suffer and die in that part of the cave. But another of Mammoth Cave’s famous ghosts has a stranger origin. Her name is Melissa. According to the story, Melissa was hopelessly in love with her tutor. Unfortunately for Melissa, her tutor was hopelessly in love with someone else. So she came up with a plan. She invited him to explore Mammoth Cave. They traveled deep underground, with Melissa carrying their only light. Passage after passage took them farther from the entrance until, once she was certain he could never find his way back alone, Melissa abandoned him. He never surfaced. Some versions say guilt eventually drove Melissa back into the cave to search for him. And somewhere along the way, she died, too. Her ghost is said to wander near Echo River, wailing as she searches for the man she left to die. It’s a true gothic (unrequited) love story. Melissa wasn’t a real murderer. She was a character in a short story. In February 1858, The Knickerbocker magazine published “A Tragedy of the Mammoth Cave.” The story was later attributed to writer Lillie Devereux Blake, who had visited Mammoth Cave with her husband. In the story, Melissa confesses that, 15 years earlier, she abandoned the man she loved deep inside the cave. At the end, the dying Melissa announces that she plans to return to the cave and await her own death there. Later retellings took it from there, turning a fictional confession into the legend of a ghost still wandering Mammoth Cave. Readers and retellers even filled in more of her biography, such as that she died of tuberculosis, mixing historical context with fiction. According to legend, her ghost still wanders the passages looking for her victim. This one isn’t just a campfire story. In Samoan culture, aitu are spirit beings that don’t neatly fit into the Western idea of a “ghost.” According to the National Park Service, belief in aitu is deeply rooted and seriously respected in Samoa, where stories of encounters with them are still shared. For generations, To’aga has been associated with them. To’aga is a stretch of beach on the island of Ofu, within what is now the National Park of American Samoa. Archaeological evidence shows people have lived in the area for thousands of years. Today, no one lives at To’aga. When National Park Service planners began studying the area before the park’s creation, people on Ofu offered very specific warnings. Don’t walk To’aga Beach at noon, and don’t walk it after dark. It’s a gathering place for Aitu. Park researchers later discovered that the same warning had been written down decades earlier in a place you might not expect to find a supernatural story—a government health report. In 1950, the Government of American Samoa’s Public Health Department recorded a series of stories surrounding a medical dispensary built at To’aga in 1923. Officials chose the location because it was convenient for residents of Ofu and nearby Olosega. People on the island objected. To’aga, they warned, was a well-known meeting place of aitu. The government built there anyway. Around 1924, according to the report, a navy medical worker stationed at the dispensary started hearing knocking at the door. He opened it, but no one was there. The knocking happened night after night. Then, one night, he opened the door and found the apparition of a headless man waiting, according to the National Park Service. The strange encounters continued. While the pharmacist’s mate was away on a call, his wife reportedly heard unseen visitors stomping through the house and moving furniture in broad daylight. Then came the story that seems to have stuck with people. One night, the worker, his wife, and others were traveling by longboat toward To’aga. Two nurses who had been with them stayed behind and planned to make the trip later. As the boat approached the beach, the group saw people gathered on the sand. A siva, a Samoan dance, was underway, but something was wrong with the dancers. They were headless. Among them, according to the report, were the two nurses the group had just left behind. The government report doesn’t present the story as proven fact, and it explicitly notes that its veracity had been disputed. But that’s almost beside the point, because the deep belief in aitu at To’aga didn’t begin with that one incident. The 1950 report says islanders already considered the area a gathering place for aitu long before the government built its dispensary there. Residents initially refused to even use the facility. Eventually, they dismantled the dispensary and moved it to Ofu village. Its foundations remain at To’aga. Decades later, when National Park Service researchers arrived, people on Ofu still gave them essentially the same warning recorded in the old report. Don’t go there at noon. Don’t go there after dark. Built in 1922, Phantom Ranch sits nearly a mile below the rim of the Grand Canyon, tucked among cottonwoods beside Bright Angel Creek. You can’t access it by road, so you can hike down, hitch a ride on a mule, or arrive via the Colorado River. Phantom Ranch has plenty of ghost stories. One of the creepiest comes from the old bunkhouse used by its mule wranglers. The National Park Service has recorded a story passed down among ranch workers about a wrangler who walked into the bunkhouse one day and saw a former mule packer standing inside. That would have been unremarkable, except she later learned that the man she saw had died there of natural causes years earlier—and that she was sleeping in the same bed where he died. Hikers and campers have also described shadowy figures walking past them, sometimes dressed in clothing that seems to belong to a bygone era—men in suits, women in ankle-length skirts. Other figures look more like ordinary hikers. They approach, ask for water and disappear. Some visitors report hearing the crunch of heavy boots crossing the gravel outside, with nobody there when they look. Even the name Phantom Ranch seems almost suspiciously perfect. But the ranch actually wasn’t named for any of these ghosts. Architect Mary Colter chose the name in the early 1920s, borrowing “Phantom” from nearby Phantom Creek and Phantom Canyon. Where those phantoms came from is harder to pin down. One story leads to a prospector named John Shane. Early Phantom Ranch caretaker Noah Kelly said Shane had been killed years earlier near the mouth of a side canyon up the creek, crushed when a rock fell from the canyon wall. Afterward, prospectors and hunters supposedly began seeing a strange light moving along the cliff near the place where he died. Kelly claimed he’d seen it himself. During a storm, he said, a light appeared on the cliff like someone carrying a lantern. It moved from place to place, disappeared, then came back again, sometimes dim and sometimes bright. And we know the story was circulating early. When a visitor named Ralph Pierson stayed at Phantom Ranch in 1926, he wrote that he and the other guests spent the evening playing cards and hoping the phantom would appear. Plenty of people, he said, claimed to have seen a whitish shape moving through the recesses of the high cliffs. But Pierson didn’t see it. The following year, a Kansas City Star correspondent arrived and heard essentially the same story. The phantom, he was told, appeared at night on the mountain as a white, veiled, roughly human figure. Unfortunately, the writer discovered that his cabin sat directly beneath the cliff where it supposedly appeared. Over the next century came the stories of the dead mule packer in the bunkhouse, figures from another era, hikers in search of water, and the sounds of footsteps belonging to no one. Unlike some other ghost stories from the national park system, the apparitions don’t seem to have been grafted onto the ranch decades later. Visitors were already looking for it in the 1920s, almost as soon as Phantom Ranch itself opened. What they saw on those cliffs is another question. Whatever it was, people have been looking for it ever since. If any hotel in a national park looks like it should have a ghost, it’s the Ahwahnee. Opened in Yosemite Valley in 1927, the grand hotel is filled with stone fireplaces, dark timber, enormous windows and soaring public rooms. In its nearly 100 years of service, it has hosted presidents, royalty and celebrities. And, according to generations of guests and employees, not everyone who checks into the Ahwahnee checks out. One of the hotel’s most famous spirits is Mary Curry Tresidder. Mary was the daughter of David and Jennie Curry, who founded Camp Curry in Yosemite Valley in 1899. She grew up there, later married Donald Tresidder and eventually helped run the Yosemite Park and Curry Company, which operated the Ahwahnee and other hotels and visitor facilities throughout the park. Donald helped develop the hotel, and in 1928, the couple moved into an apartment on the Ahwahnee’s sixth floor. When Donald died in 1948, Mary stayed. She ran the company for years and remained deeply tied to Yosemite for the rest of her life. Even after retiring, she kept her Ahwahnee apartment. In 1970, Mary went to sleep there and never woke up. And, as the stories suggest, she never entirely left. Guests and employees have reported seeing Mary’s presence around the hotel, especially near the sixth floor. In one version of the legend, guests report waking up to someone gently tucking their blankets around them. In another, Mary wakes them because she wants to dance. She isn’t the Ahwahnee’s only reported spirit. Visitors and employees have reported hearing footsteps in empty hallways and other unexplained presences around the hotel—stories the National Park Service itself describes as encounters with generally “friendly spirits.” Which is a fair categorization because a ghost that tucks you in at night and wants to dance doesn’t sound so sinister. Then there’s the rocking chair. Because what good haunted dwelling doesn’t include a creaky rocking chair? President John F. Kennedy visited Yosemite in 1962 and stayed at the Ahwahnee. According to park lore, Kennedy requested a rocking chair for his room. After his assassination the following year, stories started to circulate that the chair sometimes rocked on its own. Unlike Yellowstone’s headless bride, no one has admitted to inventing this story, and there doesn’t seem to be one clear-cut moment when the tale began. But we do have the actual history behind the ghost herself. Mary really did grow up in Yosemite. She really did help run the company behind the Ahwahnee, and she had an apartment on the hotel’s sixth floor for decades. And she really did die there in 1970. Some time after her death, the stories started to rack up. Guests felt a presence. Employees heard footsteps. Someone even woke up tucked more tightly into bed than they remembered. The woman who dedicated so much of her life to the hotel eventually became part of its folklore. Maybe that’s how a hotel gets a ghost. Someone has to love the place enough not only to want to spend a lifetime there, but also an afterlife. If the Ahwahnee already looks like the perfect setting for a ghost story, Hollywood apparently agreed. When Stanley Kubrick made The Shining, elements of the Ahwahnee’s interior were recreated for the Overlook Hotel—most recognizably its cavernous Great Lounge and elevators. It’s fitting that a hotel with its own collection of ghosts helped create one of the most famous haunted hotels in fiction. Apparently one wasn’t enough.

item.title: Fewer Airbnb chores, new adventures from Marriott and other hotel news you missed this week
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Fewer Airbnb chores, new adventures from Marriott and other hotel news you missed this week As October keeps trucking along, so does the hotel industry. The temperatures might be dropping (just like the leaves!), but things are starting to heat up in the second half of the year as new hotels open and are announced, people start gearing up for the holiday travel and plans for next year's vacations are in the works. Hilton Honors loyalists got some interesting news this week: members can now pay their checkout bill using points with the app. Initially rolling out to 150 properties, around 6,000 hotels should offer the service by next year. Marriott also made some noise with the news that it's opening another safari camp in Tanzania. Here's what else you need to know. Hilton launches new tools for businesses Hilton for Business, the company's travel program for small and medium-sized business, is rolling out new tools for customers, based on their own feedback. The changes include companies being able to book stays for employees without needing separate logins, the ability to see upcoming reservations for a team in one place, the business being able to modify or cancel reservations for employees and a dedicated way to see "employees' current in-house stays, supporting duty of care while travelers are on the road," according to a statement. More changes to ease the travel experience for companies and employees will continue to roll out in the coming months. Kimpton has a new 'Curious Palate" IHG's Kimpton brand is inviting everyone to sit around the table with its new program, "The Curious Palate by Kimpton." The program is "a new global food and beverage platform celebrating the people, places and wonderfully original ideas behind the brand's culinary culture," according to a statement. The program will feature Kimpton hotels and hotel restaurants around the world for "unexpected pairings, chef-led dining experiences and new twists on beloved Kimpton rituals." Right now, a few examples include "A Global Holiday Pour," a special spiced rum cocktail served at Kimptons created by Monika Lukasyk of Kimpton Charlotte Square in Scotland; "Fitzroy & Fries," a special martini and unlimited fry offering every day at 4 p.m. at the Kimpton Fitzroy London; and an IYKYK (if you know, you know) room service order of a banana milkshake, french fries and bubbles at the Kimpton Canary Hotel in Santa Barbara. Marriott wants to take you on a luxury expedition Marriott's brand The Luxury Collection introduced The Luxury Collection Expeditions, "a collection of journeys extending the brand's long-held role as The Destination Authority beyond the hotel stay and into the culture and character of a destination." Those expeditions are starting to shake out, and include exploring Kyoto with an artist, exploring Italy in classic cars and even a special beach fishing excursion in Turks & Caicos. Beyond Green adds new members in Costa Rica and Spain Beyond Green, a collection of sustainable-focused hotels and resorts (and part of the I Prefer rewards program), has added two exciting new members: El Silencio Lodge & Spa in Costa Rica and Hotel Món Sant Benet in Spain. In Costa Rica, El Silencio Lodge & Spa is surrounded by five protected wildlife areas and sits in a secluded cloud forest. And in Barcelona, Hotel Món Sant Benet has a Michelin-starred restaurant and is surrounded by a medieval monastery. Airbnb scales back which 'chores' guests are responsible for I've reported for a while now on Airbnb users feeling overburdened by checkout rules that, at times, go beyond what's usually expected (think: mopping the floor or washing and folding towels). Now, Airbnb is giving Airbnb Hosts (the people who list their properties) new parameters for those asks, including the ones listed below: - Dishes: Guests shouldn't be asked to wash and put away dishes, but you can ask them to put used dishes in the sink. - Laundry: Guests shouldn't be asked to remove sheets from the bed or start a load of laundry, but you can ask them to gather used towels. - Trash: Guests shouldn't be asked to take garbage off-site, but you can ask them to separate their trash and recycling into designated indoor bins. - Utilities: Guests shouldn't be asked to avoid using a listed amenity like air conditioning, but you can ask them to turn it off when they leave. The company shared that "all requests must be reasonable under the new policy," adding that "most guests want to avoid unexpected chores" and that asking guests to do tasks a "cleaner should handle" can impact their rating, according to a statement about the changes.

item.title: The haunting landscapes of England's witch country
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
'There's this spooky presence in Pendle Hill': Trace the footsteps of England's most famous accused witches The borough of Pendle has been considered haunted ever since nine suspected witches were sent to their deaths there in 1612. Here's how curious visitors can trace their steps. According to local legend, visitors to Pendle Hill are supposed to feel inexplicable feelings of anger, panic or dread. But as I reach the top of the 557m-high (1,8270ft) muddy escarpment in England's east Lancashire region, I mostly feel exhausted. And wet. Yet, surrounded by the thick mist that often envelops the summit, it's impossible to deny a sense of unease. After all, this very area is where 12 Lancastrians were accused of witchcraft in 1612, leading to one of England's deadliest witch trials. Ever since, Pendle Hill's surrounding villages and ancient forests have been considered haunted. Warning: This article contains details that some readers may find upsetting. "There are rumours of ghostly and phantom monks, while people have reportedly experienced breathing difficulties there," says Stephen Oldfield, a Lancashire historian and author. According to tour guide Stephen Entwhistle, locals claim that the last piece of snow melting on Pendle Hill takes the shape of a witch. Such tales have long lured visitors to Pendle Hill, particularly since the 400th anniversary of the trials in 2012. It's an especially popular jaunt around Halloween, when ghost-hunters try to connect with spirits allegedly haunting the borough's villages while enjoying some of the most underrated landscapes in northern England. Plan your trip: How to get there: If driving, aim for the Pendle Hill lay-by located on Barley Lane, where you can park and then walk up the hill. The Witch Way express bus also connects Manchester city centre with nearby town Burnley. When to go: Year-round, but the area's dark, wet autumns create an appropriate atmosphere of dread. Where to stay: The Pendle Inn is right in the heart of where the alleged witches terrified their neighbours. What to do: Stop at the Pendle Heritage Centre to learn about the Pendle witches and explore its 18th-Century garden. Witches Galore, in Newchurch-in-Pendle, sells witch memorabilia as well as renowned history books on the Pendle Witch Trial and other spooky local tales. In early 17th-Century England, murder via witchcraft (alleged or otherwise) was already a capital offence. But the deeply superstitious king, James I, raised the stakes even higher with the Witchcraft Act of 1604, which deemed even non-fatal witchcraft – such as conjuring spirits and casting spells – punishable by death. The elderly and the poor were especially at risk of accusations, as were "cunning folk" claiming to be healers. "This was a time of great turmoil," says Oldfield. "People were very, very suspicious of anybody who didn't live what they considered to be a normal life." The Pendle Hill witch panic began in March 1612 when folk healer Alizon Device encountered peddler John Law, who collapsed (or suffered a stroke) shortly afterward. Law's son reported Device to local magistrate Roger Nowell, who investigated the incident. Device reputedly confessed to having paralysed Law, implicating her grandmother, Elizabeth Southerns, and Anne Whittle – rival folk healers with alleged supernatural powers – as well as Whittle's daughter, Anne. All four were locked in Lancaster Castle's prison. A Good Friday gathering held at the Device home, interpreted by Nowell as a coven meeting, resulted in more arrests. Oldfield says the newly accused, including wealthy Alice Nutter of Roughlee, were kept overnight at nearby Ashlar House, then forced to walk through the Forest of Bowland to Lancaster Castle where they were thrown into Well Tower dungeon. The prisoners were collectively accused of various kinds of maleficum (malevolent magical acts), including the murder of 10 locals. Nine-year-old Jennet Device was a crucial witness, giving testimony so convincing it doomed her mother, brother, sister and grandmother. Southerns died awaiting her verdict, but nine of the 12 accused were found guilty and hanged on Gallows Hill. Only Alice Grey was acquitted; Jennet Preston was hanged in her native Yorkshire. Witch hunt fever continued for several decades more until the Age of Enlightenment, and witchcraft was eventually decriminalised in England in 1736. A 'spooky presence' The Pendle Hill trials remain some of the most famous and well-documented in English history, and the borough has never managed to shake its sinister past. Oldfield says Pendle Hill's damp, bleak landscape naturally lends itself to stories of hauntings and sightings: "There's always been this atmosphere and spooky presence in Pendle Hill. It's like being in another country, even compared to West Lancashire". Local author Stacey Halls, whose debut novel was set during the Pendle witch trials, finds being on the hill unnerving. "When you're up there on a cloudy day, which it always is up there, you literally cannot see. It's like being in a cloud… It's a bit unnatural, a bit spooky." Some local wells, like St Chad's Well near Bull Hole Farm, still have anti-witch protection marks carved into them. Television programmes, including Most Haunted and The Haunted Hunts, explore Pendle to locate spirits, especially on Tynedale Farm, where the Nutter family lived for generations. For the 400th anniversary of the Pendle witch trials in 2012, local organisations funded the Pendle Witches' Way and the Lancashire Witches' Walk, which trace the imagined routes the accused may have taken to their imprisonment at Lancaster Castle. Looking to follow in the steps of the twelve, I slip and slide back down Pendle Hill, towards hopefully drier, more solid ground that will give me a deeper sense of the region's history. I start my homage in Newchurch-In-Pendle, the tiny village where several trial victims lived. Perched steeply on the hillside, it claims only 940 residents, and "when you drive [in], it still feels very much like it would have done when the trials took place," says Oldfield. Often overlooked in favour of the nearby Lake and Peak Districts, this area of east Lancashire is equally scenic, with dramatic green hills, lush pastures and storybook cottages. "If you are looking for fresh air, stunning views all the way over to Yorkshire, and a nice walk, then the top of Pendle Hill is ideal," says Entwhistle. As I stroll through the town, I find chilling spectres of its haunted past. Several homes display witch-inspired art, while others have horseshoes on their doors and holly trees planted outside – traditional protection from spells. Signposts depicting a witch on a broomstick guide me to the trailhead of the Pendle Witches' Way, which leads me to St Mary's Church – an imposing English Gothic parish in the shadow of Pendle Hill. This churchyard is where, during her trial, Nutter was accused of having desecrated graves to rob bones and teeth. It is also the site of the Witches' Tomb, a large stone vault widely believed to belong to Nutter and her ilk. Though headstone bears the Nutter name and enigmatic carvings of a skull, Oldfield is sceptical – Nutter was a common name in the area, and a convicted witch would "never have been allowed to be buried on consecrated ground". Walking through the silent churchyard, I spot tombstones going further back in time, their names increasingly harder to read. Being so close to such unsettling history sends a shudder down my spine, so I look up at the church's tower, where I spot the unique, eye-shaped "Eye of God" carving – inscribed into the tower in the years after the trials to protect Newchurch-in-Pendle from evil spirits. I continue my quest, driving down from Newchurch-in-Pendle through the rolling Lancashire countryside – first, to the picturesque village of Barley, the primary starting point for Pendle Hill hikers, and then to Roughlee, past a life-size outdoor metal sculpture of Nutter. I then park outside Ashlar House – a gabled stone cottage in the village of Fence. "That’s the only building still standing in Pendle that we know the witches went inside," says Oldfield. Driving next through the Forest of Bowland, I am struck by the forest's dramatic valleys and wild heather fields. But any delight is curtailed as I imagine the accused's dread as they trudged the same stretch I'm now crossing in comfort. I finally arrive in the medieval city of Lancaster, the official end to both the Lancashire Witches' Walk and the Pendle Witches' Way. The 11th-Century Norman Lancaster Castle looms high on a hilltop in city centre, and I follow a handful of other tourists to the dungeon, where the accused awaited their deaths. The stone cell is damp, cramped and stifling cold – just a few moments inside is enough to make me yearn for daylight. Sorely in need of a stiff drink after all that gloom, I pop down The Golden Lion pub. According to local myth, it's where the accused had a final drink before execution, says professor Charlotte Baker of Lancaster University. Between the pub's centuries-old wooden bar and its ancient fireplace, it's easy to understand why rumours have long circulated of ghosts and strange noises emanating from the place. Publican speculation is that the noises still come from the condemned who passed it on the way to their death. Any landlord whose pub has even a passing connection to the Pendle Witch Trials – they're all likely to insist a curse took place nearby – can't wait to speak about how haunted their establishment is, says Halls. Entwhistle is unsurprised the area is increasingly inundated with dark tourists. "It's a story that should have been turned into a Hollywood blockbuster, because it has deception, lies, superstition and religion." While such fodder has helped to keep the victims' memories alive, Oldfield can't help but feel sorry for them, and the terrifying treatment they were subjected to. "These were just uneducated, poor and pitiful people, who didn't have a hope in life. Healing gave them a sense of importance. Nowadays, you'd just avoid them. But because of the atmosphere of the time, they were killed." – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.

item.title: IDEA: 5 Mysterious Places to Visit in New Hampshire’s White Mountains
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
From the world-famous UFO abduction of Barney and Betty Hill to the mountainside crash of a WWII-era bomber, the forests of the White Mountains are full of rich legends, oddities, and strange happenings alongside spectacular mountain vistas and vibrant fall foliage, making it a perfect destination for fall travel. Here are five mysterious places to visit that continue to inspire stories and legends in the White Mountain region, among locals and visitors alike. The Lore: Beneath layers of moss and decaying leaves lie rusty artifacts, scattered bricks, and the occasional stone foundation that are the only remnants of the former lumberjack town of Livermore that once stood in the area. According to local history, Livermore was incorporated during the early years of the logging industry in the White Mountains. A little less than a century later, the town would be vacant, turning Livermore into a hidden ghost town in the 20th century. How to Visit: Livermore is located off Route 302 via a hike down Sawyer River Road and can be explored through trailheads in the area. The Lore: U.S. Army plane engines, parts, and fuselage pieces twist into the ground and surrounding landscape on the side of Mount Waternomee, along with carefully placed American flags showing the crash site is still visited by hikers. A challenging trek into the forest in Woodstock reveals the wreckage of the Douglas B-18A bomber that crashed in January 1942. The bomber took off on its mission: to patrol the North Atlantic for German U-Boats during World War II. However, disaster struck on return to the airfield in Western Massachusetts as flight miscalculations and wind unexpectedly sent the plane over the White Mountains, and the bomber subsequently crashed on Mount Waternomee. Survivors were rescued by locals during a snowstorm, and the wreckage remains gnarled and woven into the surrounding mountainscape—a stark reminder of the unforgiving nature of New England terrain and weather. How to Visit: The trail is accessible via a hike down Walker Brook Road off Route 118, and the remaining wreckage commands respect for an era past. The Lore: Flashing lights, dark skies, and gray visitors from another galaxy. The connection to outer space feels a little closer in northern New Hampshire as thousands of stars illuminate the night sky with minimal light pollution. It’s no surprise the White Mountains are home to the chilling Barney and Betty Hill UFO abduction legend. According to the Hills, the couple traveled home through the White Mountains a half century ago when a white light in the sky appeared to follow them down U.S. Route 3, the primary highway through the White Mountain region. The couple observed the strange light as it zipped around before their car made an unsettling vibration sound, and the couple recalled hearing an ear-piercing beep. Shortly afterwards, the couple reported an unknown craft abducted them. Chunks of missing time and disturbing memories of the event prompted the couple to notify the Air Force the following day, and the incident became one of the most famous UFO abduction stories in the world. How to Visit: The same journey can be traveled today on Route 3, and at night, it’s even more chilling to imagine the strange light that followed the Hills as they drove through the region. The historic marker is located along Route 3 in Lincoln, and visitors can read the story on the plaque and ask themselves: What do you believe happened? The Lore: Profile Lake rests just below a towering cliff where the rock formation known as the Old Man of the Mountain stood watch over Franconia Notch before its collapse in 2003. In the early 20th century, just below the cliff stood the Profile House, a sprawling, luxurious inn that catered to travelers who visited the Old Man of the Mountain. A fire tore through the resort, leveling it, and virtually no sign that it ever existed remains. Decades later, the stone face itself crumbled after numerous attempts to secure the face to the side of the mountain failed, and the stone succumbed to the elements and time. Although the cliff face is no longer recognizable, locals continue to remember the natural oddity that inspired legends, folklore, and poetry, including a poem by writer Nathaniel Hawthorne. How to Visit: A short paved walk from the parking lot off Exit 34B on Route 93 leads to the base of Profile Lake, where the Old Man Memorial has been erected. Craggy trails wind around the lake perimeter where visitors can venture further into the woods below the jagged rock cliff and around the grounds of the old site of the Profile House. The Lore: The rocky summit of Mount Chocorua rises above the landscape in Albany and is home to the haunting legend of the Pequawket Chief Chocorua. A few variations of the story exist; the most common version ends with a white settler murdering Chief Chocorua on the mountain. How to Visit: The mountain features several moderate hiking trails looping through the region where many hikers claim to have heard haunting sounds in the woods. The area is heavily visited for its trails and panoramic views of the valley around the mountain. Whether fact or tall tale, the legend serves as a reminder of the tumultuous history of the settlement of the surrounding region. Nearby, a historic marker off Route 16 in Tamworth recounts the Chocorua Legend.
